ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A bee called Maja wants to hike from honeycomb $X$ to honeycomb $Y$. She can only move from one honeycomb to the neighbouring honeycomb if they share an edge. How many, different ways are there for Maja to go from $X$ to $Y$ if she has to step onto every one of the seven honeycombs exactly once?

Therefore it is only necessary to count Hamilton paths from A to B that pass through A,B,C,D,E,F,G once each. The white cell before B cannot be A, because A is the starting point and cannot be repeated, so it can only be D or E. Case 1: The second-to-last white cell is E, that is, the path has the form A ... Since X and Y each touch only one white cell, every valid route must begin X-A and end B-Y. Then manually enumerate Hamiltonian paths from A to B through A,B,C,D,E,F,G exactly once. Split by the penultimate cell before B: it can be D or E. Under penultimate E, list the valid paths; under penultimate D, list the valid paths. The enumeration gives 4 paths ending ...E-B and 1 path ending ...D-B, for a total of 5.
